title: Inside the Camera: Lenses, Light and Silver
summary: A camera is really just a dark box with a hole, a glass lens and something that remembers light. In this part we open the box and see how glass bends light, how silver crystals catch it, and how chemicals turn an invisible picture into a real one.

sections.heading: A Dark Box, a Hole and a Memory
paragraphs: By 1840, people had cameras, chemicals and pictures, but not many of them really understood what was happening inside. So let's take one apart. Imagine an early camera from the 1840s sitting on a wooden table: a box made of polished wood, a brass tube sticking out of the front, and a slot at the back where you slide in a plate or a sheet of paper. It looks simple, and in a way it is. Every camera ever made, from Talbot's tiny wooden boxes to the phone in your pocket, has the same three jobs.

Job one is to make an image: to gather light from the scene and arrange it into a sharp picture on a flat surface. Job two is to control how much light arrives, because too little gives a dark, murky picture and too much burns everything to white. Job three is to remember the light, which is where the silver chemistry comes in. In a phone, the memory is an electronic chip, which you will meet in Part 19. In the 1800s, it was always silver.

Start with the simplest camera of all, the camera obscura from Part 1, which is just a dark box with a small hole. Light travels in straight lines. A ray from the top of a tree passes through the hole and keeps going downwards to the bottom of the back wall. A ray from the bottom of the tree goes upwards to the top. That is why the picture comes out upside down and flipped left to right.

A pinhole has a problem, though. Each point in the scene sends a whole little cone of light through the hole, and on the back wall that cone makes a small blurry spot instead of a perfect dot. If you make the hole smaller, the spots get smaller and the picture gets sharper. But a smaller hole also lets in less light, so the picture gets dimmer. Go too small and something strange happens: light waves start to spread out as they squeeze through the tiny gap, an effect called diffraction, and the picture becomes blurry again.

Scientists have worked out the best size. For a box 50 millimetres deep, about the length of your little finger, the ideal pinhole is only about a quarter of a millimetre across, roughly the width of three human hairs. That gives a reasonably sharp picture, but a very faint one. A pinhole camera loaded with modern film can need anything from a few seconds to several hours to take a picture. For the chemicals of the 1830s, which were far less sensitive, a pinhole was hopeless. Inventors needed something that could be both bright and sharp at the same time. They needed glass.

sections.heading: Bending Light: How a Lens Focuses
paragraphs: Put a straw in a glass of water and look at it from the side. The straw seems to break where it enters the water. Nothing has happened to the straw; the light coming from it has changed direction as it crossed from water into air. This bending of light when it passes from one transparent material into another is called refraction. Light travels a little slower in glass or water than in air, and when a beam hits the surface at an angle, one side of it slows down first, which swings the whole beam round, a bit like a shopping trolley veering when one wheel runs onto grass.

A lens uses refraction on purpose. A convex lens is thicker in the middle than at the edges, like a lentil (in fact, the word lens comes from the Latin for lentil). Light hitting the outer parts of the lens meets the curved glass at a steep angle and is bent strongly towards the middle. Light passing through the centre goes almost straight. The result is that all the rays from one point of the scene, which spread out on their way to the camera, are bent back together so that they meet at a single point behind the lens. That meeting point is the focus.

This is the big difference from a pinhole. A pinhole lets through only a thin pencil of light from each point. A lens can be much wider, collecting a fat cone of light from each point and squeezing it all into one sharp dot. So a lens gives you both brightness and sharpness, which a pinhole never can.

The distance behind the lens where light from a very faraway object, such as a mountain or the Moon, comes into focus is called the focal length. Here is the important part. Closer objects focus a little farther behind the lens. Scientists describe this with a neat equation, the thin lens equation: one divided by the focal length equals one divided by the object's distance plus one divided by the image's distance. Try it with a lens of 50 millimetres focal length. A mountain far away focuses about 50 millimetres behind the lens. A friend standing one metre away focuses at about 52.6 millimetres. A flower 20 centimetres away focuses about 67 millimetres back.

That is why you focus a camera by moving the lens. Old cameras of the 1840s often had a box that slid inside another box, or a folding leather bellows, so the photographer could move the lens in and out while looking at the image on a ground glass screen at the back, a sheet of glass roughened so the picture shows up on it. Photographers draped a black cloth over their heads to block stray light and see the dim, upside-down picture clearly. When it looked sharp, they slid in the sensitive plate instead.

Lenses were nothing new. The Nimrud lens, a polished piece of rock crystal from ancient Assyria, is nearly 3,000 years old (around the 8th or 7th century BCE), although nobody is sure what it was used for. Glass reading stones, laid on a page to magnify the words, were used from about the 11th century, and spectacles appeared in northern Italy in the late 1200s. But simple lenses have a flaw: glass bends blue light a bit more than red light, so the colours focus in slightly different places and pictures get coloured, blurry fringes. This is called chromatic aberration. Around 1730 (accounts say 1729 or 1733) an Englishman named Chester Moore Hall found that by gluing together two lenses made of different kinds of glass, he could cancel most of the problem. These achromatic lenses, meaning without colour, were what made the cameras of 1839 possible.

sections.heading: The Aperture: How Wide Is the Window?
paragraphs: The aperture is the opening that lets light through the lens. You have one in each eye: the pupil, the black circle in the middle of your iris. In bright sunshine it shrinks to a tiny dot; in a dark room it opens wide to catch every bit of light it can. Try it with a mirror: close your eyes for a few seconds, open them, and watch your pupils get smaller.

Early cameras controlled the aperture with a set of metal plates, each with a different-sized hole, that slid or dropped into a slot in the lens tube. They were called stops, because they stopped some of the light. Later cameras used an iris diaphragm, a ring of thin overlapping metal blades that can open or close smoothly, like the pupil of an eye.

Photographers describe the aperture with a number called the f-number. It is simply the focal length divided by the width of the opening. A lens with a focal length of 100 millimetres and an opening 50 millimetres wide is f/2. Close the opening to 25 millimetres and it becomes f/4. The confusing part is that a bigger f-number means a smaller hole and less light.

Lenses are marked with a standard series of f-numbers: f/1.4, f/2, f/2.8, f/4, f/5.6, f/8, f/11, f/16, f/22. Each step is called a stop, and each one lets in half as much light as the one before. Why such odd numbers? Because the amount of light depends on the area of the hole, not its width. To halve the area of a circle, you shrink its width by about 0.7, which is one divided by the square root of two. Multiply 1.4 by 1.4 and you get about 2; multiply 2 by 1.4 and you get about 2.8, and so on. So going from f/2 to f/4 is two stops, which means one quarter of the light.

Now you can see why a pinhole is so dim. The best pinhole for a 50-millimetre box works out to about f/190. A good portrait lens at f/2 lets in roughly 9,000 times more light. Your own eye works at about f/2 in the dark and about f/8 in bright light.

This is exactly how the first great lens breakthrough sped up photography. Daguerre's original camera of 1839 used a fairly slow lens. In 1840, a mathematics professor in Vienna named Joseph Petzval used careful calculations to design a new portrait lens, made by the optical firm of Voigtländer. It worked at about f/3.6 and gathered roughly 22 times as much light as Daguerre's lens. Combined with more sensitive plates, it helped cut portrait exposures to under a minute in good conditions, which is why daguerreotype studios could suddenly photograph ordinary people.

The aperture changes something else too: how much of the picture is sharp from front to back, called the depth of field. With a wide aperture like f/2, only things at one distance are sharp and the background melts into a soft blur, which is lovely for portraits. With a narrow aperture like f/16, nearly everything from a flower at your feet to the distant hills can be sharp. Landscape photographers in the 1800s often used tiny apertures for this reason, even though it made their exposures longer.

sections.heading: The Shutter and the Art of Exposure
paragraphs: The aperture decides how wide the door is. The shutter decides how long the door stays open. Together they control the exposure, the total amount of light that reaches the plate or film.

In the 1840s, the shutter was usually the photographer's hand. Exposures took many seconds or even minutes, so the photographer simply pulled the brass cap off the front of the lens, counted, perhaps using a pocket watch, and put the cap back on. Nothing faster was needed, because nothing faster was possible. Only after plates became much more sensitive, in the 1870s and 1880s, did inventors need mechanical shutters that could open and close in a fraction of a second. One early example was a rapid shutter made by A. A. Pearson of Leeds in 1875.

Modern shutters come in two main types. A leaf shutter sits inside the lens and is made of thin metal blades that spring open and snap shut. A focal-plane shutter sits just in front of the film or sensor and uses two curtains that race across it, leaving a slit of light between them. Shutter speeds are marked as fractions of a second: 1/30, 1/60, 1/125, 1/250, 1/500. Each step roughly halves the time, which means it halves the light, just like one f-stop.

This is the clever part. Because both the aperture and the shutter work in halves and doubles, a photographer can trade one for the other. Suppose a picture is correctly exposed at f/8 for 1/125 of a second. You could open up one stop to f/5.6, which doubles the light, and use 1/250 of a second, which halves the time. The exposure is exactly the same. Open up again to f/4 and use 1/500. Same exposure again. So why choose one over another? A fast shutter freezes a running dog. A small aperture keeps the whole landscape sharp. Every exposure is a choice.

The third thing that matters is how bright the scene is. In bright sunlight there may be many thousands of times more light than in a candlelit room, which is why early studios had huge glass windows and skylights, often on the top floor, and why photographers worked mostly in the middle of the day. Some even used mirrors and reflectors to bounce extra sunlight onto a sitter's face.

And the fourth is how sensitive the plate or film is, which today we call film speed, or ISO. A faster film needs less light. To understand why some silver is more sensitive than other silver, we have to shrink down and look at the crystals themselves.

sections.heading: Silver Crystals and the Invisible Picture
paragraphs: Take a piece of old black-and-white film and look at it under a powerful microscope. The light-sensitive layer, called the emulsion, is not a smooth coating at all. It is a layer of gelatin, the same kind of stuff that makes jelly wobble, packed with billions of tiny crystals. These are grains of silver halide, usually silver bromide, sometimes mixed with silver chloride or silver iodide. Each grain is far too small to see with your eyes, typically around a thousandth of a millimetre across. The gelatin holds the grains in place but lets the processing chemicals soak in and out.

Each crystal is a neat, repeating pattern of two kinds of particles: silver ions, which are silver atoms that have lost an electron, and bromide ions, which are bromine atoms that have gained one. As long as nothing disturbs them, they sit happily in their pattern. Now let a bit of light arrive.

Light comes in tiny packets of energy called photons. When a photon hits a silver bromide crystal, it can knock an electron loose. That free electron wanders through the crystal until it gets stuck at a weak spot, a little flaw or a speck of impurity on the crystal, called a sensitivity speck. There it meets one of the silver ions that also roam around inside the crystal and joins with it. A silver ion plus an electron makes an ordinary silver atom. Two British physicists, Ronald Gurney and Nevill Mott, explained this process in 1938, long after photography was invented; for the first hundred years, photographers used it without really knowing why it worked.

One silver atom is not enough. It can easily fall apart again. But if more photons arrive, more atoms gather at the same spot, and once a cluster has grown to about four silver atoms, it is stable. Those few atoms are the latent image, the invisible picture from the glossary. You could look at the film all day with an ordinary microscope and see nothing. Yet the information is there, a pattern of grains with tiny silver clusters where light fell and grains without them where it did not.

The latent image is surprisingly tough. It can last for months or longer. In 1897 the Swedish explorer S. A. Andrée and two companions set off to fly over the Arctic in a hydrogen balloon and never returned. When their last camp was found in 1930, their exposed film was developed, about 33 years after the pictures were taken, and some images still appeared.

Grain size matters, too. Bigger crystals catch more photons, so they reach that magic four-atom cluster with less light, which makes the film faster. But big crystals also make the picture look grainy, like sand. Fine-grained film shows more detail but needs more light. Photographers have always had to choose between speed and sharpness.

sections.heading: In the Darkroom: Developer, Stop, Fixer, Wash
paragraphs: Now for the magic trick. Step into a darkroom: a room with no windows, a sink, trays of liquid, and a dim red or orange safelight glowing in the corner. Ordinary black-and-white printing paper is hardly sensitive to red light, so you can see what you are doing without spoiling it.

Step one is the developer. This is a chemical that can turn silver halide into pure metallic silver. The clever part is that it works far, far faster on crystals that carry a latent image. Those four or so silver atoms act like a seed: once the developer starts at that spot, it converts the whole crystal, billions of silver atoms, into a tiny black clump of metallic silver. That makes the developer a chemical amplifier, multiplying the effect of light by up to billions of times. Grains that saw no light stay untouched, at least for a while. Common developing chemicals include metol and hydroquinone, mixed with an alkaline chemical to make them work. Early photographers had their own: Daguerre used mercury fumes, and Talbot used gallic acid from oak galls.

Timing matters. If you leave film in the developer too long, it eventually starts turning even the unexposed grains black, and the whole picture fogs over grey. So after a few minutes you move on to step two, the stop bath, a weak acid, often similar to dilute vinegar, that halts the developer almost instantly.

Step three is the fixer, the hypo that Herschel discovered. The developed areas are now metallic silver, which light cannot change any more. But the unexposed areas are still full of light-sensitive silver halide, and if you carried the film into daylight now, it would slowly darken all over. The fixer, sodium thiosulfate or a close relative, latches onto those leftover silver halide grains and turns them into a substance that dissolves in water. After fixing, nothing light-sensitive remains, and the picture is safe in daylight.

Step four is washing, and it is more important than it sounds. If fixer chemicals stay in the film or paper, over the years they can stain the picture yellow or brown and eat away the silver. That is exactly what happened to many early prints, including some of Talbot's, which faded because nobody yet knew how carefully they had to be washed. Museums today recommend thorough fixing and washing for any picture meant to last a century. Finally, the film is hung up to dry, often with clothes pegs on a line.

So what is a black-and-white photograph really made of? Countless microscopic clumps of pure silver metal, embedded in gelatin. Where there are many clumps, the picture looks black; where there are few, it looks grey; where there are none, you see the clear film or white paper underneath.

sections.heading: Flipping the World: Negatives and Positives
paragraphs: Think about what that means for a picture of a sunny garden. The bright sky sent lots of light to the film, so it is full of black silver. A dark green hedge sent little light, so it is mostly clear. A white cat is black; a black cat is clear. That is the negative, with every tone reversed.

To get a normal picture, you do the whole process a second time, on paper. In a contact print, you lay the negative directly on top of a sheet of light-sensitive paper, press it flat under glass, and shine light through. Where the negative is dark, as in the sky, little light reaches the paper, so the paper stays white. Where the negative is clear, as in the hedge, lots of light gets through and the paper turns dark. After developing and fixing the paper, the tones are flipped back to normal. Two reversals make a positive, just as two minus signs in maths make a plus.

This is exactly what Talbot did with his calotypes, laying waxed paper negatives on salted paper in the sunshine. A contact print is always the same size as the negative, so if you want a bigger picture you need a bigger negative. That is why some Victorian photographers lugged around enormous cameras with plates as large as a newspaper page.

Later, photographers used an enlarger, which is really a camera working backwards. A lamp shines through the negative, and a lens projects a magnified image of it down onto a sheet of paper on a baseboard. Move the head up and the picture gets bigger. With an enlarger, a tiny negative can become a poster, which is what made small cameras practical in the 20th century.

Some processes skip the negative altogether. A daguerreotype is a direct positive: the image formed on the silver plate is the final picture, which is why every daguerreotype is one of a kind. Bayard's paper photographs of 1839 were direct positives too. Colour negatives, which came much later, reverse the colours as well as the brightness, so a blue sky looks orange-brown and red lips look greenish. But the principle is still Talbot's: make one negative, then print it as often as you like.

sections.heading: Try It Yourself: Pinholes and Sun Prints
paragraphs: You do not need a darkroom to see this science in action. Here are two safe experiments to try with an adult.

First, a pinhole viewer. Take a long cardboard box, such as a cereal box, or a tube. Cut a square hole at one end and tape a piece of aluminium foil over it. Prick a single small, neat hole in the foil with a pin. At the other end, tape a sheet of white paper inside to act as a screen, and cut a viewing hole in the side near that end. Point the pinhole at a brightly lit window or a sunny street, put your eye to the viewing hole and cover your head with a dark cloth. You will see a faint, upside-down, colourful image of the world on the paper. Try making a second, bigger hole and compare: brighter, but blurrier. You have just rediscovered the camera obscura from Part 1. The same viewer lets you watch a solar eclipse safely, because you look at the projected image on the paper, never at the Sun itself. Never look at the Sun directly, through the pinhole or through any lens, binoculars or camera.

Second, a sun print. Toy shops, science shops and craft stores sell sun print paper, which is usually cyanotype paper, the same blue process Herschel invented in 1842 and Anna Atkins used for her seaweed. It is pre-coated, so you do not handle any chemicals yourself. Indoors, away from bright light, arrange flat objects on the paper: fern leaves, keys, lace, paper cut-outs. Cover with a sheet of clear plastic or glass from a picture frame to hold them flat. Carry it into bright sunshine for a few minutes, until the paper fades to a pale colour. Then rinse it in a bowl of plain water for a minute or so and let it dry. Your objects appear as crisp white shapes on deep blue.

Notice what you have made. The parts that saw sunlight turned dark blue; the parts that were covered stayed white. It is a negative, just like Talbot's leaves. Rinsing with water does the job of fixing, washing away the chemicals that did not react, so the picture will no longer change in the light. Even with no special paper at all, you can see light at work: leave a sheet of dark construction paper in a sunny window for a week with a few coins on it, and you may find pale paper with dark coin shapes where the light faded the dye.

So now we know the whole secret: a lens to make a bright, sharp image, an aperture and a shutter to control the light, silver crystals to catch a hidden picture, and chemistry to bring it out and fix it. But in the 1840s, the material holding those crystals was still the weak point. Paper was cheap and could make copies, but its fibres made every picture fuzzy. Metal daguerreotype plates were beautifully sharp but could never be copied. What if you could have both? What if you coated the silver onto something perfectly clear and smooth, something like glass?

deepDive:
The numbers behind exposure are all about doubling and halving, which is why photographers count in stops. One stop is a factor of two in light. The f-number series goes up by about 1.41, the square root of two, because light depends on the area of the aperture, which grows with the square of its width. A lens at f/2 therefore delivers four times the light of the same lens at f/4. Shutter speeds, film speeds and even lighting are all measured in the same factor-of-two steps, so a photographer can swap one for another without doing any real arithmetic.

The pinhole shows the physics of light most clearly. For a pinhole of diameter d at distance f from the screen, a bigger hole blurs the image by simple geometry, while a smaller hole blurs it by diffraction. The best balance falls at a diameter proportional to the square root of f times the wavelength of light; the mathematician Joseph Petzval, designer of the 1840 portrait lens, worked out a version of this in 1857 and Lord Rayleigh another in 1891. For a 50-millimetre pinhole camera the optimum is about 0.26 millimetres, giving an f-number near 190, roughly 13 stops slower than a portrait lens at f/2.

The silver chemistry was not properly explained until 1938, when Ronald Gurney and Nevill Mott proposed that light frees electrons in a silver halide crystal, that these electrons gather at sensitivity specks, and that mobile silver ions join them to build up atoms of metallic silver. Later work, notably by J. W. Mitchell, showed that the positive holes left behind also matter. Experiments suggest a stable latent image needs a cluster of at least about four silver atoms. Development then converts the whole grain, billions of atoms, giving an amplification of up to several billion times. This enormous built-in amplifier is why developing-out processes such as the calotype and later film were so much faster than printing-out processes that waited for light alone to darken the silver.

There is one more surprising fact: in very heavy overexposure, film can show an image even without developing, the old printing-out effect returning. Experimenters have shown that 35mm film given an enormous overexposure, millions of times more light than normal, can show a visible picture straight out of the camera, with no developer at all.
funFact: When the lost 1897 Arctic balloon expedition of S. A. Andrée was found in 1930, its exposed film was developed about 33 years later, and pictures still appeared.

check.q: In a darkroom, what does the fixer do?
check.a: It removes the unexposed silver halide so the picture stops changing in light
wrong: It makes the hidden picture appear for the first time
It adds colour to a black-and-white image
It bends light to focus the picture
